title: Jensen Huang Said "Stop Learning to Code" — Then Hired 10,000 Developers
summary: Junior developer critiques Jensen Huang's 'stop learning to code' claim against Nvidia's own engineer hiring; IBM tripling junior hiring.

assertions.quote: suddenly this man is hiring several thousand software engineers complaining he's 10,000 short on headcount

verdicts.note: Nvidia, Meta and AI labs continued growing engineering headcount through 2025 while executives forecast automation; their behavior contradicts the strong form of the claim.

assertions.quote: If you don't bring in early talent now, you won't have mid-level or senior engineers in 5 to 10 years

verdicts.note: A straightforward pipeline argument made by IBM and others; the long-run effect is unmeasured yet but well reasoned.

assertions.quote: by May of 2025, Klarna was quietly hiring humans again

verdicts.note: There are reports of AI-motivated cuts being reversed (e.g. Klarna support staff) and analyst forecasts of rehiring, but broad 'boomerang' rehiring of engineers is weakly evidenced.

assertions.quote: experienced developers using AI actually worked 19% slower

verdicts.note: Accurately reports METR's July 2025 RCT (16 devs, ~19% slower); the finding is specific to that setting and early-2025 tools.
METR RCT: 16 experienced developers, 246 tasks in their own mature repos; allowing early-2025 AI tools increased completion time by 19%.

METR Feb 2026 restates the early-2025 result (tasks took 19% longer with AI, CI +2% to +39%) but adds that the 10 returning developers are now estimated ~18% faster with AI (CI -38% to +9%), so the slowdown was specific to early 2025.

assertions.quote: they were only needed a couple of senior developers

verdicts.note: Hiring data (e.g. Stanford 'canaries' 2025) shows junior roles hit harder than senior, but evidence that senior demand rose is weaker.

assertions.quote: It is unacceptable to say, Oh, the AI did it

verdicts.note: Ownership and maintainability require understanding; it's a reasonable review standard rather than an empirical finding.

Crossover experiment, 69 participants (mostly students): after AI-assisted tasks people answered fewer questions about their own just-written code correctly (median 87.5% vs 100%; AME -5.95 pp, OR 0.58). The authors argue this can stop contributors defending their choices in code review. That supports the reason behind the norm, but no merge gate was tested.

assertions.quote: learn to code. Learn the fundamentals

verdicts.note: Studies show novices accept incorrect AI code more often; verifying output requires domain and code literacy.
The review concludes that skill in verification, constraint specification and review may matter as much as authoring skill, and that the central risk is a verification gap.
